claims.text: The low-Al baseline is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic, disordered, single-phase FCC or BCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni solid solution with minimal ordering.
Moderate Al additions to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni cause ordered B2-like nanoscale precipitates to emerge in a disordered matrix.
Atomic ordering stabilizes the overall alloy by counterbalancing the configurational entropy favoring the disordered state.
Ordered precipitates strengthen the alloy through precipitate hardening and defect pinning.
The Al-induced ordered microstructure retains high ductility or toughness from cryogenic to high temperatures.
Increasing Al raises the importance of favorable ordering enthalpy relative to configurational entropy and thereby triggers local atomic ordering.
Ordered precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and consequently enhance high-temperature strength.
Ordered precipitates provide stable sites for irradiation-defect annihilation.
Relative to the low-Al baseline, moderate-Al alloys will have greater elevated-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the low-Al baseline, moderate-Al alloys will have lower irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Relative to the low-Al baseline, moderate-Al alloys will maintain or improve cryogenic toughness.
Low-Al, disordered single-phase baseline alloys have lower high-temperature yield strength but potentially high cryogenic toughness.
Low-Al baseline alloys have less radiation tolerance than moderately Al-alloyed variants.
Above a suitable Al-content window, detrimental phase segregation or embrittlement can occur.
The hypothesis is restricted to near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys under standard processing routes.
Failure of increased Al to produce ordering, or failure of ordering to correlate with all expected property improvements, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: An exactly equiatomic five-component alloy necessarily contains 20 at.% Al, so describing the baseline as both equiatomic and low/minimal in Al is inconsistent with treating moderate Al addition as the controlled compositional change. A specific non-equiatomic baseline is needed to resolve this.
